facts.claim: The Mixtral paper (2024) says each token has access to 47B parameters but uses only 13B active parameters while the model runs.
Mixtral’s authors found no obvious split of experts by topic (ArXiv papers, biology, philosophy); the router follows syntax more, such as Python’s “self” or English words like “Question”.
Mistral AI says Mixtral 8x7B has 46.7B total parameters but uses only 12.9B per token: 8 experts per layer, 2 chosen for each token.
Mistral AI says Mixtral 8x22B uses only 39B active parameters out of 141B: 8 experts per layer, 2 chosen for each token.
DeepSeek-V3’s report (2024) describes a mixture of experts with 671B total parameters, 37B activated for each token: 256 routed experts and 1 shared per layer, 8 routed chosen per token.
The Llama 3 paper (2024) lists its 70B model as dense: 80 layers, model width 8,192, every weight used for every token.

Kaplan and colleagues (2020) estimate that running a transformer on one token takes about two operations (a multiply and an add) for each of its weights, so a dense model’s work per token grows with its size.
Lu and colleagues (2024) removed 2 of Mixtral 8x7B’s 8 experts in each layer at random, so its router had to pick from the other six: its average score on eight tests fell from 67.58 to 63.04.
NVIDIA’s H100 page (checked 2026-10-30) lists 80 GB of GPU memory on the H100 SXM card.
Shazeer and colleagues (2017) introduced the sparsely gated mixture-of-experts layer: a gating network picks a few experts per example, so capacity grows without the compute growing with it.
Switch Transformers (2021) give each expert a capacity of tokens per batch, set by a capacity factor; tokens past it are dropped and pass on through the residual connection.
Switch Transformers add a load-balancing loss during training that pushes the router to spread tokens evenly across experts.
